text: What is tokenisation?
reference_answer: Splitting text into the units a model actually operates on. Those units might be words, characters, or subword pieces. Every downstream step depends on it, so a tokeniser that splits differently at training and serving time quietly breaks the whole system.
expected_points: splitting text into units the model processes
units may be words, subwords or characters
it is the first step in any text pipeline
the same tokeniser must be used at training and inference

text: What does a bag-of-words representation throw away?
reference_answer: Word order, and with it grammar and most of the meaning that depends on structure. It keeps only which words appeared and how often, so 'the dog bit the man' and 'the man bit the dog' become identical vectors.
expected_points: it discards word order
it keeps only word counts or presence
sentences with different meaning can be identical
syntax and structure are lost

text: What's the difference between stemming and lemmatisation?
reference_answer: Stemming chops affixes off with rules, so it is fast but can produce non-words. Lemmatisation uses a vocabulary and the word's part of speech to return the real dictionary form. Lemmatisation is more accurate and considerably slower.
expected_points: stemming strips affixes using rules
stemming can produce non-words
lemmatisation returns a real dictionary form
lemmatisation is more accurate but slower

text: What is a word embedding?
reference_answer: A dense vector representing a word, learned so that words used in similar contexts end up near each other. Unlike a one-hot vector it is compact and carries similarity — the geometry of the space encodes something about meaning.
expected_points: a dense vector representation of a word
learned from the contexts a word appears in
similar words are close in the space
far more compact than one-hot encoding

text: What are stop words, and should you always remove them?
reference_answer: Very common words like 'the' and 'is' that carry little topical meaning. Removing them helped bag-of-words models by cutting noise. For modern contextual models it is usually harmful, because those words carry grammatical signal the model uses.
expected_points: very common words with little topical content
removed to reduce noise in count-based models
removal can destroy meaning, as in negation
modern contextual models generally keep them

reference_answer: Start with a strong baseline: TF-IDF features into logistic regression. It trains in seconds, is easy to inspect, and is surprisingly hard to beat on small datasets. Only once that is measured would I try a fine-tuned transformer and see whether the gain justifies the cost.

text: What is named entity recognition?
reference_answer: Finding and classifying the spans in text that refer to real-world things — people, organisations, locations, dates. It is a sequence labelling problem, because the label belongs to a span of tokens rather than to the document.

classifying them into types such as person or location

text: What problem does TF-IDF solve that raw word counts do not?
reference_answer: Raw counts are dominated by words that appear everywhere, which carry no discriminating information. TF-IDF scales each count down by how many documents contain the word, so terms common across the corpus are damped and terms distinctive to a document stand out.
expected_points: raw counts are dominated by ubiquitous words
inverse document frequency down-weights common terms
distinctive terms get higher weight
it improves retrieval and classification over raw counts

text: Why do modern models use subword tokenisation?
reference_answer: It is the compromise between a word vocabulary, which cannot handle anything unseen, and characters, which make sequences far too long. Subwords keep frequent words whole and break rare ones into known pieces, so nothing is ever out of vocabulary.
expected_points: word-level vocabularies cannot handle unseen words
character-level sequences become very long
frequent words stay whole, rare words are split
it eliminates out-of-vocabulary tokens

text: How does word2vec learn its embeddings?
reference_answer: By training a shallow network on a fake task: predict a word from its neighbours, or the neighbours from the word. Nobody wants the predictions — the weights learned along the way are the embeddings, and they capture context because that is what the task rewarded.
expected_points: it trains on a prediction task over context windows
skip-gram predicts context from a word, CBOW the reverse
the learned weights are the embeddings
the prediction task itself is discarded

text: What do contextual embeddings give you that word2vec does not?
reference_answer: A different vector for a word depending on the sentence it is in. Word2vec assigns 'bank' one vector averaging every sense of it. A contextual model produces one vector for a river bank and another for a savings bank, because it encodes the surrounding words.
expected_points: static embeddings give one vector per word type
that vector blends all senses of the word
contextual embeddings depend on the surrounding text
polysemous words get different vectors per context

text: What does an encoder-decoder architecture do?
reference_answer: The encoder reads the whole input and builds a representation of it. The decoder generates the output one token at a time, conditioned on that representation and on what it has produced so far. It is the standard shape for translation and summarisation.
expected_points: the encoder builds a representation of the input
the decoder generates output tokens one at a time
generation is conditioned on the encoded input
it suits translation and summarisation

text: How does semantic search differ from keyword search?
reference_answer: Keyword search matches the literal terms, so a query phrased differently from the document finds nothing. Semantic search embeds both into a vector space and ranks by similarity, so it can match meaning across different wording — at the cost of sometimes matching things that merely feel related.
expected_points: keyword search matches literal terms
semantic search compares embeddings
it matches meaning across different wording

text: What do BLEU and ROUGE measure, and what is their weakness?
reference_answer: Both compare generated text to reference text by overlapping n-grams — BLEU leans towards precision for translation, ROUGE towards recall for summarisation. The weakness is that a correct paraphrase using different words scores badly, so they measure surface overlap rather than meaning.
expected_points: both measure n-gram overlap with a reference
BLEU is precision-oriented, ROUGE recall-oriented

text: What is perplexity?
reference_answer: A measure of how surprised a language model is by text it did not train on. Lower means the model assigned higher probability to what actually came next. It is useful for comparing language models on the same data, but it does not tell you whether output is useful.
expected_points: it measures how well a model predicts unseen text
lower perplexity means better prediction
it is derived from the likelihood of the held-out text
it does not measure usefulness or factual accuracy

text: Why do transformers need positional encodings?
reference_answer: Because self-attention treats the input as a set — it computes the same thing regardless of the order of the tokens. Without an explicit signal for position, the model could not distinguish two sentences with the same words in a different order.
expected_points: self-attention is permutation invariant
it has no inherent notion of token order
position must be injected explicitly
otherwise reordered sentences look identical

text: What does multi-head attention buy you over a single attention head?
reference_answer: Each head learns its own projection, so different heads can attend to different kinds of relationship at once — one tracking syntax, another coreference. A single head has to average all of that into one attention pattern, and the average is worse than the parts.
expected_points: each head learns its own projection
different heads capture different relationships
they attend in parallel and are concatenated
a single head must average all relations together

text: How does BERT's training objective differ from GPT's?
reference_answer: BERT masks tokens in the middle and predicts them using context from both sides, which makes it good at understanding but not at generating. GPT predicts the next token from the left only, which makes generation natural but means each token sees no future context.
expected_points: BERT predicts masked tokens using both directions
GPT predicts the next token from left context only

text: Why does the pretrain-then-fine-tune recipe work so well?
reference_answer: Pretraining uses enormous amounts of unlabelled text to learn general language structure, which is the expensive part. Fine-tuning then adapts that to a specific task with a comparatively tiny labelled set, because the model only has to learn the task, not the language.
expected_points: pretraining uses abundant unlabelled text

fine-tuning adapts them with little labelled data

text: Why not just average word embeddings to represent a sentence?
reference_answer: You can, and it is a reasonable baseline, but averaging discards order and lets common words dominate. Two sentences with opposite meaning but shared vocabulary land in nearly the same place. Models trained directly on sentence similarity do much better.
expected_points: averaging discards word order

text: How would you classify a document longer than the model's context window?
reference_answer: Either shorten the input or aggregate over pieces. Truncation is the cheap option and often fine when the signal is at the start. Otherwise split into chunks, encode each, and pool the results — or use a model built for long contexts if the signal is genuinely spread throughout.
expected_points: truncate when the signal is concentrated early
split into chunks and encode each

text: How do modern models handle a word they have never seen?
reference_answer: Subword tokenisation means they never truly see an unknown word — it gets split into known pieces, right down to bytes if necessary. The model then composes a representation from those pieces, which works well for morphology and badly for genuinely novel proper nouns.
expected_points: subword tokenisers split unknown words into known pieces
byte-level fallback guarantees coverage
the representation is composed from the pieces
it works better for morphology than for novel names

text: What preprocessing mistakes quietly damage an NLP pipeline?
reference_answer: Lowercasing when case carries meaning, stripping punctuation that marks sentence boundaries or negation, removing stop words before a contextual model, and — most damaging — preprocessing differently at training and serving time.
expected_points: lowercasing when case is meaningful
removing punctuation that carries structure or negation

text: Why was attention added to sequence-to-sequence models originally?
reference_answer: Because the encoder had to compress an entire sentence into one fixed vector, and that bottleneck got worse as sentences got longer. Attention let the decoder look back at every encoder state and weight them per output token, removing the bottleneck.
expected_points: a fixed-size vector was an information bottleneck
performance degraded on longer sequences
attention lets the decoder access all encoder states
weights are computed per output token

text: Where does bias in a language model come from, and what can you do?
reference_answer: From the training corpus, which reflects who wrote it and what they wrote. It shows up as skewed associations and uneven quality across groups. Mitigations exist at every stage — curating data, tuning the objective, filtering outputs — but the first requirement is measuring it per group rather than reporting one aggregate number.
expected_points: it originates in the training corpus
it appears as skewed associations or uneven quality
measure performance separately per group
mitigate through data curation, training or output filtering

text: What is hard about a single model serving many languages?
reference_answer: Capacity is shared, so adding languages can degrade the ones already there. Data is wildly unbalanced, so low-resource languages get little signal. And the tokeniser is usually fitted mostly on high-resource text, so other languages consume far more tokens for the same content.
expected_points: model capacity is shared across languages

low-resource languages perform worse

text: How would you evaluate a summarisation system properly?

Beyond that I would measure the dimensions that actually matter separately — is it faithful to the source, does it cover the key points, is it readable — with human ratings on a sample and a model-based faithfulness check at scale. Hallucination will not show up in ROUGE at all.
expected_points: overlap metrics are a weak proxy

text: How would you build search over a few million documents?
reference_answer: A hybrid. Lexical retrieval catches exact terms, identifiers and rare words that embeddings blur; dense retrieval catches paraphrase. text: What is a corpus, and why does its composition matter?
reference_answer: The body of text a model is trained or evaluated on. Composition matters because everything the model knows about language comes from it - the domain, the register, the era and the demographics of whoever wrote it all end up baked into the model's behaviour.

text: Why does text have to be turned into numbers at all?
reference_answer: Because models do arithmetic, and words are not numbers. Every NLP system starts by mapping text to a numeric representation - counts, or learned vectors - and the quality of that representation puts a ceiling on everything downstream.

text: What is a language model, at its simplest?
reference_answer: Something that assigns probabilities to sequences of words - in practice, predicting what comes next given what came before. Everything from an old n-gram model to a modern transformer is doing that same job at different levels of sophistication.

text: What is text normalisation, and when can it hurt?
reference_answer: Standardising text before processing - lowercasing, stripping punctuation, collapsing whitespace. It helps count-based methods by merging variants. It hurts when the thing you removed carried meaning: case distinguishes names, and punctuation carries negation and sentence structure.

text: What do you trade when choosing a tokeniser's vocabulary size?
reference_answer: A large vocabulary keeps more words whole, so sequences are shorter and cheaper, but the embedding table grows and rare tokens are seen too seldom to learn well. A small one splits more aggressively, giving longer sequences but better-trained pieces.

text: Why do simple text models get negation wrong?
reference_answer: Because bag-of-words style representations drop word order, and 'not good' keeps the strong positive word. Stop word removal often deletes the negation outright. Contextual models handle it far better because the representation of a word depends on what surrounds it.

text: What is zero-shot text classification?
reference_answer: Classifying into categories the model was never trained on, by describing the labels in natural language instead of learning them from examples. text: Why does sequence length matter so much in NLP?

text: What makes named entity recognition hard on real text?
reference_answer: Ambiguity and novelty. The same string is a person, a place or a company depending on context; entities span several tokens and the boundaries are arguable; and new names appear constantly, so the model must generalise from form and context rather than recall a list.

text: Why are language models unreliable with numbers?
reference_answer: Partly because tokenisation splits them arbitrarily - the same quantity can be one token or four depending on the digits - so there is no consistent representation of magnitude. And the training objective rewards plausible continuations, which for arithmetic is not the same as correct ones.

text: A model trained on news does badly on customer support chats. Why?
reference_answer: Different distribution in almost every respect - vocabulary, spelling, length, register, and the way meaning is carried. Chats are short, misspelled and full of domain shorthand the model never saw. It is domain shift, and the fix is in-domain data rather than a bigger model.
expected_points: vocabulary and register differ between domains

text: How does multi-label text classification differ from multi-class?
